parole.significato: Used to make feminine forms of some masculine nouns, or to indicate the wife of a man with a certain profession; -ess
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -issa, from Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa). Cf. also the doublet -esă, a neologism borrowed from French.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person singular present of some -a (first conjugation) verbs. E.g. lucrezi from luc…
parole.testo: Form of the infix -ez-; probably from a Vulgar Latin *-idiās or *-izās, conjugated forms of *-idiō, *-izō, ultimately from Ancient Greek -ίζειν (-ízein), used in Romanian conjugated forms of verbs. See -ez.

parole.significato: to sniff, scent, sense or trace through smell (an animal, person, etc.)
parole.testo: Unknown. Cognate with Aromanian ulmic, ulmicari. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *adosmicāre, from *adosmāre, from Ancient Greek ὀσμάω (osmáō), which would make sense semantically but is difficult to connect phonetically. Compare Italian ormare, Spanish husmear, husmar probably coming from a Latin
Inherited from Latin āēr.

Inherited from Latin daphne, with loss of initial 'd', from Ancient Greek δάφνη (dáphnē, “laurel”); cf. also Calabrian afina ("laurel"). Another theory suggests Latin acinus, influenced by daphne. See also the related dafin.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ammagīre from *magīre, *magāre, from Ancient Greek μαγεύω (mageúō, “cast a spell; bewitch”), from μάγος (mágos, “magical”); cf. also Latin magus. May be related to Catalan amagar (“hide”) and Spanish amagar (“threaten”), Portuguese esmagar, Sicilian ammagari, although th
Inherited from Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βασιλική (basilikḗ). Doublet of the borrowing bazilică. Compare Aromanian bisericã / bisearicã.

Uncertain. Possible etymologies: * If an internal development, augmentative of boroacă (“swelling”) inherited from Latin verrūca (“wart”), or a cognate of Italian brocca, inherited from Vulgar Latin *brocca, borrowed from Ancient Greek πρόχοος (prókhoos, “vessel for water”). * Borrowed from Hungaria
From an older form *băteza, from Vulgar Latin baptidiāre, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptīzāre, from Ancient Greek βαπτῑ́ζω (baptī́zō, “immerse, baptize”).

Inherited from Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos, “antelope, wild ox”). It may have passed through a Vulgar Latin intermediate form or was influenced by bubulus; cf. the form bobulum. Compare also Albanian buall. Doublet of bivol, which came through a Slavic source.
Inherited from Latin brachium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *brothācus, from Ancient Greek βροτάχος (brotákhos), from βάτραχος (bátrakhos). Compare Aromanian broatic, Albanian bretk, bretkosë.

Probably from a Late Latin bombax or *bombacum, ultimately from Ancient Greek βάμβαξ (bámbax). Compare Medieval Latin bombacium (Byzantine Greek βαμβάκιον (vamvákion)), from Ancient Greek βάμβαξ (bámbax), Italian bambagia, Venetan bombàxo, bombàs, also Greek βαμβάκι (vamváki), μπαμπάκι (bampáki), Se
Inherited from Latin bōlētus, probably through an intermediate Vulgar Latin root *boletis. Ultimately from Ancient Greek βωλίτης (bōlítēs).

parole.significato: barrel, cask; contents of a barrel
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin buttis, probably of Ancient Greek origin.
From Latin cadus, from Ancient Greek κάδος (kádos), possibly through Proto-Slavic *kadь. Compare Aromanian cadã, Albanian kadë, Aragonese cado, cadollo, Spanish cadozo.

Inherited from Latin charta, possibly through a hypothetical earlier Romanian intermediate form *cartă, and created from its plural (thus deriving its meaning from "many papers"). Ultimately from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs). Doublet of cartă, a borrowing, as well as hartă, from Greek, and hârtie,

parole.significato: shaft of a knee-high boot (the upper part that extends from the ankle to the knee)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *calamulus, from Latin calamus, from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos). Compare Spanish carámbano.

Borrowed from Latin castaneus (19th century), possibly earlier via Ancient Greek κᾰ́στᾰνᾰ (kắstănă). The Aromanian (cãstãnj) and Megleno-Romanian equivalents of the word are likely directly inherited from Latin.
Borrowed from Latin cedrus, from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros). Doublet of chedru.
Inherited from Latin circus, from Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos). Compare circ, a borrowed doublet.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin citera, from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára). Compare Italian cetra. Doublet of chitară (from Italian), țiteră (from German); cf. also the related citolă (from French).
Learned borrowing from New Latin chiro-.
From Latin cichōria, plural of cichōrium, from Ancient Greek κιχόριον (kikhórion).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), and ultimately possibly of Anatolian origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ceresius, from Late Latin cerasius, from Latin cerasus, from Ancient Greek κέρασος (kérasos). Compare Aromanian ciresh, tsiresh.

Probably from Latin cyma, from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma, “swell, wave, billow”). The meaning was probably derived from the swellings from diseases such as the bubonic plague. Compare also Aromanian ciumã (“peak, summit”), which has a meaning shared by most other Romance languages, and Albanian qime.

parole.significato: a wooden bucket used to get water from a well
parole.testo: From an alteration of Latin cotyla, cotula, from Ancient Greek κοτύλη (kotúlē). Cognate to Megleno-Romanian ciutură, Aromanian ciuturã, ciutrã, Italian ciotola.
Inherited from Latin coma, from Ancient Greek κόμη (kómē).
Inherited from Latin chorda, from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string of gut, cord”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōleum n, from Latin cōleus m, of Ancient Greek origin. Compare Aromanian colj, coalji.
Inherited from Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós). Doublet of horă.

Inherited from Latin Christiānus, itself from Ancient Greek Χρῑστιᾱνός (Khrīstiānós). The sense of "person" is also found in many other Romance cognates. Doublet of cretin and hristian. Compare Aromanian crishtin, crãshtin.
Inherited from Late Latin cucus or cuccus. Compare Ancient Greek κόκκυξ (kókkux), Classical Latin cuculus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *clubium, from Ancient Greek κλυβίον (klubíon). Compare Aromanian cuib.

Inherited from Latin corōna, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē). Doublet of coroană, which was a borrowing. The /r/ to /n/ phonetical evolution is due to a hypercorrection of the rhotacisms which existed in some dialects of Old Romanian.
Borrowed from Late Latin cuprum, contraction of Latin (aes) Cyprium (literally “brass of Cyprus”), from Ancient Greek Κύπρος (Kúpros, “Cyprus”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin cottizāre or cottidiāre (compare Aromanian cutedz, cutidzari, Megleno-Romanian and Istro-Romanian cutez, Venetan scotezàr, Istriot cutisà, Aquileian scuttia, compare also Albanian kuxoj), from Ancient Greek κοττίζω (kottízō, “to play craps, shoot dice”).

Inherited from Late Latin, Vulgar Latin canapa, *canapis (compare Aromanian cãnipã, Italian canapa, Dalmatian canapial (“cord”)), from Latin cannabis, from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). Doublet of canabis.

parole.significato: in groups of, in series of (used to indicate a collective or distributive numeral, and often used with a number)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin cata, from Ancient Greek κατά (katá). The normal result in old Romanian would have been *cată, later *cate, and was influenced by cât (see the above etymology). Compare Spanish and Portuguese cada, Occitan cadun, French chacun, Italian cadauno.

Inherited from Latin capisterium, probably through a Vulgar Latin *capisteria. The Latin further derives from Ancient Greek σκαφιστήριον (skaphistḗrion). Compare Tuscan Italian capistejo, capisteo, Abruzzese Neapolitan capistiera.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cascāre, from Ancient Greek χάσκω (kháskō, “to yawn, gape”). Compare Aromanian hascu, cascu, Sardinian cascare, cascai.

parole.significato: laurel (evergreen shrub, of the genus Laurus)
parole.testo: Probably from Late Latin daphinus, from Ancient Greek δάφνη (dáphnē). Also possibly from Serbo-Croatian dafina; other theories suggest this word was actually borrowed from Latin or Romanian. See also the related afin.

parole.significato: to reel on/up, wind a hank of something on a reel or bobbin
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *depānāre or *depēnāre, from Latin pānus (“thread wound upon the bobbin”), from Ancient Greek πῆνος (pênos). Compare Aromanian deapin, dipinari, Italian dipanare, Catalan debanar, Spanish devanar, Portuguese dobar, Sardinian demanare.
Inherited from Latin doga, from Ancient Greek δοχή (dokhḗ), from Proto-Indo-European *doḱ-éh₂.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”).

Inherited from Latin dracō (“dragon”), from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn). Compare also Catalan and Occitan drac and the derived French drac. Doublet of dragon, which was borrowed from French. Compare Sicilian dragu, Megleno-Romanian and Aromanian drac.
Borrowed from Latin ethos or Ancient Greek ἦθος (êthos).
Inherited from Latin pharmacum, from Ancient Greek φάρμακον (phármakon, “a drug, charm, enchantment”), from φαρμακίς (pharmakís, “witch”).
Borrowed from Latin gamba, from Ancient Greek κάμπη (kámpē).

parole.significato: Greek (of or pertaining to Greeks, the Greek language or the Greek culture)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin graecus, from Ancient Greek Γραικός (Graikós).

From a Vulgar Latin root *grylliolus, from Latin gryllus, from Ancient Greek γρύλλος (grúllos, “performer in an Egyptian dance, comic figure, caricature”). The Vulgar Latin form would have normally yielded Romanian *greior initially, followed by later changes; another more likely explanation starts
Inherited from Latin cotōneus, from cotōneum, from Ancient Greek κυδώνιον (kudṓnion).

From gutui (“quince tree”), or less likely a Vulgar Latin root cotōnea, taken as a feminine singular from the plural of Latin cotōneum, ultimately from Ancient Greek κυδώνιον (kudṓnion). Compare Italian cotogna, Sicilian cutugna; compare Latin māla cotōnea < mālum cotōneum.
Uncertain. Possibly ultimately from Late Latin gamba (“leg”), from Ancient Greek κάμπη (kámpē), or an alteration of găbui, which has the same meaning.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gamphae, from Ancient Greek γαμφαί (gamphaí), variation of γαμφηλαί (gamphēlaí, “jaw of an animal”).
Learned borrowing from Latin historia or Ancient Greek ἱστορίᾱ (historíā). First attested in the 17th century.
Inherited from Latin gȳrus, from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros). Doublet of girus.
Inherited from Latin marmor, borrowed from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros).

Inherited from Latin martyr, or Vulgar Latin martur, from Ancient Greek μάρτυρ (mártur). Compare Old Italian martore, Sardinian màrturu (“invalid”), Calabrian marture, Lombard màrtul (“saint”). Or directly from Greek. Doublet of martir.

Inherited from Late Latin mixticius (“of mixed race”), translation of Ancient Greek σύμμεικτος (súmmeiktos, “commingled”), from Latin mixtus, past participle of misceō (“to mix”). Compare Spanish mestizo. Doublet of metis, which was borrowed from French.
Borrowed from Latin monachicus or Ancient Greek μοναχικός (monakhikós). By surface analysis, monah + -ic.
Inherited from Latin mōrus, from Ancient Greek μόρον (móron).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin mora, from Latin morum, from Ancient Greek μόρον (móron). Compare Italian mora, French mûre, Catalan móra, Spanish mora.
From Early Medieval Latin mustācium (via its plural mustācia), ultimately from Ancient Greek μύσταξ (mústax). Compare Aromanian mustatsã.
Borrowed from Latin musica, borrowed from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “art of the Muses”), derived from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manganeāre or *manganiāre, from Ancient Greek μαγγανεύω (manganeúō); see μάγγανον (mánganon, “charm”).

parole.significato: rage, great anger, wrath, ire, fury, craze, mania
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin mania, from Ancient Greek μανία (manía). Doublet of manie.
Inherited from Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”). Compare Aromanian oarfãn, Spanish huérfano. Largely replaced by the form orfan from Greek.
Inherited from Latin hōra, from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “time, season, year”). Doublet of oră, which was a borrowing.
Borrowed from Latin oleum, from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”). Doublet of ulei.
Borrowed from Latin horologium, from Ancient Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion).
Borrowed from Late Latin orthodoxia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxía, “right opinion”). By surface analysis, ortodox + -ie
Borrowed from Latin hōra (“hour”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “time, season, year”). Cognate to the inherited doublet oară.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plātinus, from Latin platanus (“plane tree”), itself from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos); same change of meaning in Albanian panjë (“sycamore maple”). See also Romanian platan, an etymological doublet stemming from the same Greek word.

parole.significato: rush, bulrush, club-rush, cattail, reed mace (Typha)
parole.testo: Inherited from a Vulgar Latin *papura, from Latin papȳrus, from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros). Doublet of papir and papirus. Compare Megleno-Romanian papră.
Borrowed from Latin paradoxum or Ancient Greek παράδοξος (parádoxos).
Probably inherited from Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Compare Italian parola, cf. also Albanian përrallë. Doublet of parabolă, parolă, and palavră.
Inherited from Latin pepō, peponem, possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *pepinem, or a later Romanian innovation. The Latin derives from Ancient Greek πέπων (pépōn). Compare Aromanian peapini.
From Latin periodus, Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos), French période.
Borrowed from Latin periodicus or Ancient Greek περιοδικός (periodikós) or French périodique. By surface analysis, period + -ic.
Inherited from Latin petra (“stone, rock”), from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra).

parole.significato: a thick flour made from grain, mixed with cornflour, or used to fry meat with
parole.testo: Probably from Latin pegma, from Ancient Greek πῆγμα (pêgma, “anything fastened or joined together; anything congealed”). The Romanian word's meaning seems to be more closely derived from the more abstract original Greek sense, as the Latin sense refers more to a specific object like a bookcase or fi
Borrowed from New Latin placenta, from Latin placenta, from Ancient Greek πλακόεντα (plakóenta). Compare also the doublet plăcintă, inherited from the same source.

parole.significato: plateau; flat raised area or expanse of terrain
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plagium, ultimately from Ancient Greek πλάγιος (plágios). Compare Albanian pllajë. Compare Latin plagia, whence came Italian spiaggia / piaggia, French plage (and the borrowed Romanian doublet of plajă (“beach”)), Spanish playa, Portuguese praia.

parole.significato: traditional pie or pastry (savory or sweet, often filled with cheese and fruit, and coming in various forms, sometimes…
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin placenta, from Ancient Greek πλακόεντα (plakóenta). Doublet of the borrowing placentă. Compare Aromanian plãtsintã.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin preb(i)ter or prev(i)ter, popular variant of Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros). Compare Albanian prift, Aromanian preftu, preft, Italian prete, French prêtre, Catalan prevere. Doublet of prezbiter.
Inherited from Latin prūnus, from Ancient Greek προύνη (proúnē).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *prūna, feminine singular formed from the neuter plural of Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦμνον (proûmnon).
Inherited from Latin paliūrus, from Ancient Greek παλίουρος (palíouros).

parole.significato: a rough homespun woolen fabric (used to make coats, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin paenula, from Ancient Greek φαινόλη (phainólē).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *palanga, from Latin phalanga, from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx). Compare Italian and Spanish palanca, French planche. Doublet of palancă and falangă.
Ultimately from Latin petroselīnum, from Ancient Greek πετροσέλῑνον (petrosélīnon, “parsley”), from πέτρος (pétros, “rock, stone”) + σέλῑνον (sélīnon, “celery”).
Borrowed from Latin rhetorica or Ancient Greek ῥητορική (rhētorikḗ) or French rhétorique.
Probably a 17th-century learned borrowing from Latin rūta; ultimately from Ancient Greek ῥυτή (rhutḗ).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rhonchizāre (“to snore”) (compare Old Italian roncheggiare, Istriot ronchizea), from Latin rhoncō, rhonchāre (compare Spanish roncar), denominative of rhonchus (“snoring”), from Ancient Greek ῥόγχος (rhónkhos).
Inherited from Latin resīna, from Ancient Greek ῥητῑ́νη (rhētī́nē). Compare Albanian rrëshirë.
Inherited from Latin saccus, from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “sack, bag; sackcloth”), ultimately of Semitic origin.
Inherited from Latin scōria, from Ancient Greek σκωρία (skōría). Doublet of the borrowing scorie, as well as the more common zgură, taken from Greek.
Inherited from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “broad blade”). Compare also the borrowed doublet spadă and espadă.
Borrowed from Latin spongia, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá), from σπόγγος (spóngos). Probably a doublet of spânz.
Borrowed from Latin stibium.
Borrowed from Latin stomachus (“gullet, stomach”), from Ancient Greek στόμαχος (stómakhos, “throat, gullet, stomach”). Compare Albanian stomak. Compare Aromanian stumahi, stumahe

parole.significato: barn owl (An owl of the genus Tyto)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin strīga, from strix, from Ancient Greek στρίξ (stríx).
Inherited from Latin struppus, stroppus, from Ancient Greek στρόφος (stróphos, “rope”), from στρέφω (stréphō, “to twist”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *strambus, from Latin strabus, from Ancient Greek στρᾰβός (străbós), akin to Aromanian strãmbu, Albanian shtrembër, Italian strambo, Friulian stramp, Spanish zambo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *stypus or *stupus, from Ancient Greek στύπος (stúpos, “stem, stump, block”).

parole.significato: tow (untwisted bundle of fibers such as hemp or flax)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin stuppa, from Ancient Greek στύππη (stúppē).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sambata, from Vulgar Latin *sambatum, from Latin sabbatum. The Latin is derived from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton, “Sabbath”), ultimately from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát, “Sabbath, Shabbat”). Compare French samedi (“Saturday”), itself also from *sambatī diēs. Compare als
Inherited from Latin thēca, from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē, “a case, box, receptacle”).
Borrowed from Latin tetrarches or Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs) or French tétrarque.
Inherited from Latin toxicum, from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón, “arrow poison”), from τοξικός (toxikós, “pertaining to bows”), from τόξον (tóxon, “bow”).
From a Vulgar Latin root *thȳmānea, from Latin thȳmiāma, from Ancient Greek θυμίαμα (thumíama). Compare Sardinian timanza, timagna, Old French timoine; cf. also Aromanian timnjamã.
Probably from a Latin orgia, from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia). Doublet of orgie.

parole.significato: to follow (go where someone else goes, not in pursuit)
parole.testo: From urmă, perhaps connected to a Vulgar Latin root *osmāre, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ). Compare Italian ormare, ormeggiare, also Spanish husmear, husmar, Old French osmer, Venetan usmar. Also compare adulmeca.

Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *orma or Late Latin osma, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ) . Compare Aromanian urmã, Megleno-Romanian urmă, Istriot urma, Italian orma, also Spanish husma, Venetan usma and Friulian olme.

It could be directly inherited from Latin zema (“saucepan”). However, it is more likely that the word is from Ancient Greek ζέμα (zéma, “decoction, something boiled or fermented; extract; essence”), through a Vulgar Latin intermediate *zema. The current meaning in Eastern Romance is closer to that o
Inherited from Late Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos). Doublet of Anghel.

parole.significato: (usually wooden) rod or bar, especially those used to hold together or form a net
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin schidia, from Ancient Greek σχίδια (skhídia).
